idea-plugin.name: Flow Lens
idea-plugin.description:
Flow Lens turns a selected function into an explorable map of what runs next. Put the caret in a method, run Analyze Flow, and read the execution path forward from there. Every step leads back to the source.

It is a reading tool for unfamiliar code, debugging, review, and onboarding. It is not a repository-wide analyzer and not a runtime tracer: it follows explicit calls in the source, within a depth and node budget you control, and marks every place it stopped rather than trailing off.

What it shows

  • Real evaluation order. save(convert(load())) reads as load, then convert, then save — not as the order the text is written in. Chained calls follow the receiver chain; arguments evaluate left to right.
  • Control flow as structure. Conditions, switches, loops, and try blocks are drawn as containers with labelled branches, and the sequence resumes after them instead of hanging off one branch.
  • Uncertainty, stated rather than hidden. Every call carries a resolution status and a dispatch confidence. A virtual call that may be overridden at runtime says so; an interface call with no single responsible continuation stops rather than guessing — and you can choose which implementation to follow, with the card still reporting the confidence it actually has.
  • Asynchronous timing. A lambda, a Kotlin trailing lambda, or a Go closure handed to a call becomes a step of its own with a body you can open, and it says when it runs: in place, concurrently, as a goroutine, deferred — or that the timing could not be determined, which is stated rather than left for you to assume.
  • Somewhere to work from. Pin the functions you keep returning to, save a flow together with the limits it was analyzed at, re-open recent ones, and export any flow as Markdown or as a Mermaid diagram for a review or an issue.

Languages: Java, Kotlin, and Go (Go requires the JetBrains Go plugin). One flow may cross Java/Kotlin boundaries, because the analyzer is chosen per resolved target rather than once for the whole run.

Where it runs: Flow Lens needs an IDE with Java support. It is developed and verified against IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate; other JetBrains IDEs may work but are not verified targets.

Local-first: no AI service, no server, no network calls. Nothing you analyze leaves your machine, and the logs hold counts and timings rather than your source.
idea-plugin.change-notes:
1.0.0 — First release.

  • No new capability, and that is the point: the feature set is settled, and 1.0 is about the one thing Flow Lens does being dependable. From a selected function, it maps execution forward and shows the uncertainty and the analysis boundaries rather than hiding them.
  • Everything below shipped during development and is listed so you can see what the plugin grew from.

0.5.0 — Asynchronous semantics.

  • A body handed to a call — a lambda, a Kotlin trailing lambda, a Go closure — is no longer invisible. It appears as its own step, with its own frame you can open, named after the call it was given to.
  • Each one says when it runs, in words: in place, concurrently, as a goroutine, deferred — or that the timing could not be determined. Flow Lens states an unknown timing rather than letting position imply an answer, and the status area counts the ones it could not justify.
  • Go parity: go func() { … }() and defer func() { … }() bodies are now visible.

0.4.0 — Ambiguity and sharing.

  • An interface or abstract call is no longer a dead end: Flow Lens lists the implementations the project contains and follows the one you choose. The call still reports the dispatch confidence it actually has — a choice is not a proof — and says whose body it is showing.
  • Export a flow as Markdown or as a Mermaid flowchart, carrying the same uncertainty the canvas shows, so a map can go into a review or an issue.

0.3.0 — Developer workflow.

  • Flow Pins: mark a function and it stands out in every flow that reaches it, across restarts.
  • Saved Flows: keep an entry point with the limits it was analyzed at, and re-run it later exactly as it was.
  • Recent analyses: the last ten entry points, one click away.
  • Analyze from Here: promote the selected call's target to the new root.
  • A running analysis now names the callable it is working on and shows how much of the node budget is spent; a finished one summarizes why its map stops where it does, and each count leads to the card.

0.2.0 — Control flow on the map.

  • Branches, multi-way branches, loops, and exception handling are now part of the map: a structure is one container with labelled sections, and the sequence visibly resumes after it.
  • Java if/switch/loops/try, Kotlin if/when/loops/try, and Go if/switch/select/loops, plus return and throw as terminal markers.
  • A repeated call appears once inside its loop container instead of being duplicated outside it.
  • The "control flow simplified" disclosure now appears only for control flow that is genuinely not represented, such as a short-circuit operand or a break, rather than on every branch.

0.1.0 — Multi-language method flow and Flow Canvas.

  • Analyze a Java, Kotlin, or Go function into an explorable flow map; analysis crosses Java/Kotlin boundaries per resolved target.
  • Evaluation-order call extraction for nested, chained, and argument calls; call sites stay distinct from target symbols.
  • Resolution and dispatch classification: project, external, unresolved, built-in; exact, declared target, ambiguous, unknown.
  • Go goroutine and defer semantics preserved; compiler-generated declarations are never followed as authored code.
  • Progressive local-first canvas with nested frame expansion, cycle, depth-limit and node-limit markers, project-boundary crossings, selection details, and target / call-site navigation.
  • Bounded cancellable analysis off the EDT, with indexing wait and stale-source handling; project-scoped settings; English and Japanese UI.
